title: Charts that tame large rates, and what they cost: a log coordinate, its dead zone, and a power chart
summary: Replacing a state by its logarithm or a power of it changes the vector field the solver and the optimizer see. These figures show the standard facts about such charts: relative rates replace absolute ones, a clamp creates a zero-gradient dead zone, a power chart compresses eigenvalues but amplifies errors on the way back, and the spectral radius of the transformed field is bounded below by the largest relative rate.

media.alt: Three panels in a row. Left, a 3D orbit titled ROBER orbit in log coordinates, drawn as a coloured curve from deep purple (early) to yellow (late) in log10 y1, log10 y2 and log10 t. Middle, titled the shift diag(f over y): relative rates of three species against time on log axes. Right, titled spectrum moves under the log map: eigenvalue magnitudes against time for the raw Jacobian (solid) and the log-chart Jacobian (dashed).

read_the_figure.question: What does the chart do to the rates (eigenvalues) of the problem, and what does it hide or break?
read_the_figure.axes: Log-coordinate orbit: log10 of species concentrations and log10 of time (colour). Relative rates: time (log) against the relative rate of each species (symlog). Spectrum: time (log) against eigenvalue magnitude (log). Dead zone: prediction over epsilon, or parameters on log axes with colour showing the fraction of dead samples. Power chart: raw eigenvalue magnitude against compressed or amplified quantities, p between 0.05 and 1.
look_at: Relative rates (middle panel): in the log chart the field is f_i / y_i, so species that start tiny have enormous relative rates that fall as they grow; this shift is added to the Jacobian.

Spectrum (right): the raw eigenvalues (solid) and the log-chart ones (dashed) agree after the transient but are very different at early times; the log chart replaces the small raw eigenvalue by a large one.

Spectral radius bound (last panel of the group): the spectral radius of the log-chart Jacobian follows max(rho(J), max_i |f_i / y_i|) closely: the points lie near the diagonal of a log-log parity plot.

Dead zone: below the clamp level the loss is flat and the gradient zero; the parameter map is black where the prediction stays below epsilon for every sample, so Adam cannot move; the additive-epsilon variant has no such region.

Power chart: the raw eigenvalue is compressed to its p-th power (orange dots) at a price: an error in z is amplified by 1/q in y, growing with the eigenvalue (bars on the right panel); and the chart is singular at the equilibrium y = 0, where dz/dy = q y^(q-1) diverges.

Smooth charts and the spectral radius along a trajectory: a ratio of spectral radii close to one for random charts and a dip for a chart chosen for a time window; the trajectory spends most of its time near the fixed point.
read_the_figure.proves: A chart can reduce stiffness only by moving the relative rates, and a log chart cannot reduce them below the relative rate of the fastest species. Every compression has a price in the inverse map, and a hard clamp creates a region where learning stops.
if_wrong: A clamp inside the data range: gradient is zero for part of the data.
Relative rates of order 1e6 at early times: the log chart is more, not less, stiff there.
A compressed eigenvalue shown without the amplification of errors in the inverse: only half the cost is reported.
A chart singular at an equilibrium that the trajectory approaches: the late-time field is infinite.
must_check: That the clamp level or epsilon is stated and below the data range.
That the raw and transformed spectra are plotted on the same axes.
That the price of a compression (error amplification) accompanies its benefit.
That singularities of the chart relative to the dynamics are discussed.

terms.meaning: z = ln y: the field becomes the relative rate of change.
The rate divided by the state; the natural scale for positive quantities spanning decades.
A region where a transform has zero derivative so no gradient reaches the parameters.
z = y^q with q between 0 and 1; compresses large magnitudes.
The largest eigenvalue magnitude of the Jacobian.

remember: For z = ln y the Jacobian is J_z = Y^{-1} J Y - diag(f_i / y_i).
Hence the spectral radius of the log chart is of the order of max(rho(J), max |f_i / y_i|).
A clamp max(y, eps) has derivative zero below eps; ln(y + eps) is smooth.
A power chart with q below 1 compresses eigenvalue magnitudes but its inverse amplifies errors by 1/q.
A chart that is singular at an equilibrium (y = 0) cannot describe the approach to it.

steps.title: The log chart Jacobian
steps.note: The first term is a similarity transform of the raw Jacobian (same eigenvalues); the second is the shift diag(f/y) that the middle panel plots.

steps.title: Why the spectral radius cannot fall below the relative rate
steps.note: When one species decays or grows quickly in relative terms, the shift dominates the spectrum. This is the empirical parity statement of the parity panel.

steps.title: The dead zone of a clamp
steps.note: With a loss on g, parameters that push all predictions below epsilon receive zero gradient and stay there (the black region). The additive form keeps a nonzero slope.

steps.title: The price of a power chart
steps.tex: z=y^{q}\ \Rightarrow\ y=z^{1/q},\quad \delta y=\frac1q\,z^{1/q-1}\,\delta z,\qquad \frac{\mathrm dz}{\mathrm dy}=q\,y^{q-1}\to\infty\ (y\to0)
steps.note: Compressing the rate by raising to the power q means the inverse magnifies errors; and the chart's own slope diverges at the equilibrium, so the late-time field of the chart is singular.

worked.title: Relative rate of a tiny species
worked.problem: A species has y = 1e-8 and absolute rate f = 4e-4 per second. Find its relative rate and compare with a raw eigenvalue of 1e3 per second.
worked.answer: 40 times the raw eigenvalue: in the log chart the spectral radius at that moment is about 4e4, not 1e3.

analyze.q: In the middle panel the relative rate of species 2 falls by many decades after t of 1e-2. Why?
Why is the black region in the dead-zone map a trap for Adam but not an obstruction for the additive epsilon?
What does the amplification 1/q in the price panel imply for the accuracy of predictions mapped back from z to y?

evaluate.q: Does a log chart make a stiff problem easy? State when it helps and when it makes things worse.
evaluate.hint: Relative rates of species near zero.

evaluate.q: A chart is tuned to reduce stiffness in one time window. What should be reported alongside?
evaluate.hint: Behaviour outside the window; inverse errors.

create: Write the log-chart field for a two-species decay y1' = -k y1, y2' = k y1 and find its Jacobian.
Plot ln max(y, eps) and ln(y + eps) for eps = 1e-3 and say which you would use inside a loss.

checks.q: What is the field of z = ln y?
Why does a clamped log stop learning below epsilon?
checks.answer: Because its derivative is zero below epsilon, the gradient of the loss with respect to the parameters vanishes there.

checks.q: A power chart reduces the largest eigenvalue by a factor 1e3. Is the problem 1e3 times easier?
checks.answer: Not necessarily: errors in the chart are amplified in the inverse and the chart is singular at the equilibrium; the net benefit must be measured by end-to-end error and cost.

checks.q: Propose a figure that shows both benefit and cost of a chart.
checks.answer: Plot the spectral radius of the chart and the error amplification of the inverse against time on the same log axis.
